analysis.one_liner: Locks in cheap 40-year federal water contracts for California farm districts and lifts Delta endangered-species protections.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 246–175 on February 29, 2012, but the Senate never voted on it, and it died when the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill rewrites the rules for California's federal Central Valley Project. At a contractor's request, the Interior Secretary would have to renew their long-term water delivery contracts for 40 years, only charge for water actually delivered, let them pay off remaining construction costs at a discounted Treasury rate, and free them from federal reclamation law limits on price and acreage. It would require the project and the State Water Project to be run under a 1994 water quality agreement "without regard to" the Endangered Species Act or any other law, and would preempt stricter California conservation rules. It also stops implementation of the 2006 court settlement to restore the San Joaquin River, cuts payments to the project's restoration fund, and lets water be transferred between users without the Secretary imposing mitigation conditions [S3] [S4].
analysis.who_benefits: The large agricultural water contractors that buy subsidized federal water in the Central Valley — mainly irrigation districts in the San Joaquin and Sacramento valleys. They would get guaranteed minimum deliveries even in dry years (100% of contract amounts in wet through below-normal years, 75% in dry years, 50% in critically dry years for Sacramento River watershed contractors), 40-year contract renewals on request, the option to pay off remaining construction costs at a discounted Treasury rate, and freedom from reclamation law limits on price and acreage once they pay off. Kettleman City, a small disadvantaged community, would gain a contract for up to 900 acre-feet of municipal water. Water marketing is also made easier: transfers can no longer carry mitigation requirements [S3] [S4].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Central Valley irrigation districts and farm water contractors

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Secretary to renew existing Central Valley Project water contracts for 40 years at the contractor's request (up from the current 25), and to charge only for water actually delivered [S3] [S4].

Lets contractors convert repayment contracts to pay remaining construction costs at a discounted Treasury rate, after which federal reclamation law pricing and acreage limits no longer apply to their lands [S4].
Guarantees Sacramento River watershed agricultural contractors at least 100% of contract amounts in wet, above normal, and below normal years, 75% in dry years, and 50% in critically dry years [S4].

Requires the Central Valley Project and State Water Project to be operated under the 1994 Bay-Delta Accord "without regard to" the Endangered Species Act or any other law, and bars the state from restricting any water right to protect a species affected by the projects [S3] [S4].

Directs the Secretary to cease implementing the 2006 San Joaquin River restoration settlement and cuts restoration fund fees, including capping fund payments for project power at $4 per megawatt-hour [S3] [S4].
Adds the Kettleman City Community Services District to the project's authorized service area with a contract for up to 900 acre-feet of water for municipal use [S3] [S4].

analysis.who_pays: The San Joaquin River and Sacramento–San Joaquin Delta ecosystems, and the commercial and recreational salmon fisheries and Delta communities that depend on them, since the bill would run the projects without regard to the Endangered Species Act and other environmental laws and cut restoration funding. The state of California would lose regulatory authority over its own waters, since the bill preempts stricter state rules and restricts conditions on state water rights. Taxpayers bear costs that shift away from contractors, from reduced restoration fund collections to discounted repayment of construction costs [S3] [S4].
analysis.who_pays_short: Salmon fisheries, Delta communities, and California's state authority

drawbacks.text: Operating the two largest water projects in California without regard to the Endangered Species Act and Bay-Delta protections would reduce the flows that salmon and other native fish need, hurting an already-depleted fishery [S3] [S4].

The bill preempts California's own endangered species and water quality rules for the projects and bars the state from restricting any water right, including pre-1914 rights, to protect species or public trust values — an unusually broad assertion of federal supremacy over state water law [S3] [S4].

Repudiating the 2006 San Joaquin River settlement would unwind a court-approved agreement that farmers and environmental groups had already negotiated, and eliminating mitigation requirements on water transfers removes a check on third parties being drained by transfers [S3] [S4].

The restoration fund provisions waive the requirement that at least 67% of fund money go to habitat restoration, cap fund payments, and bar fund fees as a condition for storing or moving non-project water, shrinking the money available for the fish and habitat mitigation the project owes [S3] [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers real, long-term financial value to a small set of federal water contractors: guaranteed deliveries, 40-year contracts, and a discounted buyout path out of reclamation law limits. The costs fall broadly — on the Delta ecosystem and salmon fishery, on communities that depend on state water quality enforcement, on California's authority over its own water, and on taxpayers who absorb costs contractors would otherwise repay. Because the gains are concentrated and the costs are spread across the environment, the state, and the treasury, and because the state itself already had a negotiated alternative, the bill's design favors its main beneficiaries far more than any statewide water solution.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 246–175 in February 2012, but the Senate placed it on its calendar and never voted on it, so it died when the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The House Natural Resources Committee ordered the bill reported on a 27–17 vote on February 16, 2012, and reported it amended on February 27 [S6].
The House passed the bill on a recorded vote of 246–175 with 1 present on February 29, 2012 (Roll no. 91); 236 of 241 Republicans voted yes and only 10 of 192 Democrats did [S8].

A Democratic motion to recommit the bill with instructions — to add a section titled 'Protecting the Constitution and States' Rights' — failed 178–248 (Roll no. 90), with all 178 voting Democrats in favor and no Republicans [S7].
Amendments from California Democrats (Thompson, McNerney, Garamendi, Napolitano, Markey) all failed during floor consideration [S6].
The Senate received the bill on March 1, 2012, and placed it on its legislative calendar, but no vote was ever taken; the bill died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Central Valley water contractors did not get the statute they wanted, but no one lost water or money to its provisions. California's salmon fishery, Delta communities, and state authority over its own water are better off because the bill never became law; the House vote itself handed the sponsoring Central Valley Republicans a talking point without a binding result.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: California's Delta, salmon fishery, and fishing communities

industries.industry: Central Valley irrigation districts and CVP agricultural water contractors
industries.note: The bill would lock in these contractors' subsidized federal water for 40-year renewable terms, guarantee minimum deliveries, and let them buy out of reclamation law price and acreage limits at a discounted rate. Their gain comes at the cost of the river and Delta ecosystems, the fisheries they support, and costs shifted to taxpayers.

industries.industry: Commercial and recreational salmon fishing industry
industries.note: Running the Central Valley Project and State Water Project without regard to the Endangered Species Act and cutting restoration funding would reduce the flows salmon need, shrinking harvests for fishing businesses and the coastal communities that depend on them.

industries.industry: Water marketing and water transfer brokers
industries.note: The bill requires the government to expedite transfers and bars the Secretary from imposing mitigation or other requirements on them, making it easier and cheaper to move subsidized water to the highest bidder; the removed mitigation checks are the public's protection.

A genuinely helpful provision: the bill adds this small disadvantaged community to the project's service area with a contract for up to 900 acre-feet of drinking and municipal water, at non-federal cost for infrastructure.
